#694. 128,000-year-old ice in Tibet could rewrite climate history

Deep within an ice cap in northwestern Tibet, scientists have uncovered evidence of a remarkable frozen record that may stretch back more than 128,000 years. The discovery suggests that ice high in the mountains has survived since the last ice age and could provide an extraordinary window into Earth's ancient climate.

The findings extend the known glacial record from the region by more than 100,000 years, making these the oldest ice cores ever recovered from this part of Tibet. They also offer rare evidence of how mountain glaciers endured major changes in Earth's climate.

Researchers reached their conclusions by examining ice cores collected from the Guliya Plateau in 1992 and 2015. Despite being drilled 23 years apart, the samples revealed strikingly similar patterns of oxygen isotopes, which scientists use to reconstruct past environmental conditions. The close match indicates that the ice has preserved a reliable and reproducible record of climate history.

"Reproducibility of the records within a given ice cap is extremely important," said Lonnie Thompson, lead author of the study, professor of earth sciences and senior research scientist at the Byrd Polar Research Center at The Ohio State University. "If you get an identical record a quarter of a century later, it can tell you a lot about the behavior of the ice over time."

How Scientists Dated the Ancient Tibetan Ice

Determining the age of ice that has remained frozen for tens of thousands of years is no simple task. To establish a more accurate timeline, the international research team turned to advanced dating methods involving radioactive isotopes of beryllium and chlorine.

These naturally occurring radioactive forms of elements decay at predictable rates, making them valuable tools for identifying events deep in Earth's environmental history. In this case, researchers used them to detect evidence of the Leschamp Geomagnetic Excursion, a dramatic disturbance in Earth's magnetic field that occurred more than 41,000 years ago and left distinctive chemical signatures in the ice.

The team then compared its findings with oxygen isotope records preserved in nearby Tibetan cave deposits. Together, the evidence suggests that the Guliya ice record may extend well beyond 128,000 years into the past.

"It's a really critical finding, because outside of the polar regions, this is the only ice core we have from the mountaintops that go back that far," he said. "Records out of Huascarán only go back over 30,000 years, not over 100,000, so that makes Guliya a very unique record."

The findings were published in the journal Science Advances.

A Frozen Climate Record From the Last Ice Age

Ice cores are among scientists' most valuable sources of information about ancient climates. As snow accumulates and gradually becomes compressed into ice, it can preserve chemical clues about the atmosphere and environmental conditions at the time. By examining different layers, researchers can piece together how climate changed over thousands of years.

However, interpreting these records depends on knowing when each layer formed. Without a reliable timeline, even an exceptionally well-preserved ice core can be difficult to understand.

That uncertainty had complicated earlier interpretations of the Guliya ice cap. Previous research suggested that its record reached back only to the middle of the Holocene, the geological epoch that began nearly 12,000 years ago following the last ice age.

The new evidence establishes that at least some of the ice is considerably older than the Holocene. This also has important implications for understanding whether large ice masses in Tibet persisted as the planet emerged from the last glacial period.

"If we only had Holocene-era ice in Tibet, that would mean that the big ice sheets from the last ice age didn't persist through the early Holocene," said Thompson. "But evidence shows that it did."

What the Discovery Reveals About Earth's Glacial History

The Guliya ice cap's unusual geography may help explain why it has preserved such an exceptionally old climate record. Its high elevation and surrounding terrain likely contributed to conditions that allowed ancient ice to remain in place through major environmental changes.

Beyond establishing the ice's age, researchers hope that a more precise timeline will help answer fundamental questions about the history of Earth's glaciers. Knowing when major periods of glaciation began, how long they lasted, and when the ice retreated is essential for reconstructing the planet's natural climate cycles.

"When did ice start forming on the planet and what did those natural processes of loss look like?" said Thompson. "We need to know those things, and the only way you can really demonstrate it is with accurate time scales on these records."

The revised timeline also creates new opportunities to investigate the Guliya ice cores in greater detail. Researchers plan to study additional samples to determine how other indicators of past climate and environmental conditions fit into this much longer history.

Those future analyses could reveal information that was previously overlooked or interpreted differently because scientists did not fully understand the age of the ice.

For Thompson, one of the most encouraging aspects of the discovery is how consistently the different measurements support the same interpretation.

"The big picture is that our results tell a very consistent story," he said. "If you get the science right, it's consistent. It's our understanding of what it's trying to tell us that has to catch up."

The research received support from the U.S. National Science Foundation. Ohio State co-authors include Mary Davis and Ellen Mosley-Thompson. Other contributors were Juerg Beer of the Swiss Federal Institute of Aquatic Science and Technology; Christof Vockenhuber and Marcus Christl of ETH Zurich in Switzerland; Tandong Yao of the Chinese Academy of Sciences; and Ninglian Wang and Ling Fang of Northwest University in China.

#693. Pam Abdy Laments Exits of Top Female Executives in Hollywood: “It Is Upsetting to See”

Abdy, who was ousted as Warner Bros. co-film chief after Paramount Skydance completed its $111 billion acquisition of the studio, received Women in Film’s inaugural Vanguard Award on Thursday night.

By Mia Galuppo, Kirsten Chuba November 5, 2026 7:38pm

At Thursday night‘s Women in Film Honors, Pamela Abdy was on hand to receive one of the evening’s big awards, one month after being ousted as the film chief at Warner Bros.

“I have been relaxing and taking a breath and taking a minute and hanging out with my family,” Abdy told The Hollywood Reporter on the event‘s red carpet of what she has been up to in the past month, adding that her family was with her at the night‘s event, including her mother and daughter.

At this year‘s WIF Honors, Abdy is receiving the inaugural Vanguard Award, a recognition for a leader whose career embodies the qualities that move the industry forward, and is set to be presented the award by Nancy Meyers. Meyers worked with Abdy on her latest feature film, Paris Paramount, the beloved filmmaker‘s first time back in the director’s chair since 2015‘s The Intern. Related Stories Business Skydance Reveals Key TV and Streaming Leadership Roles Business George Cheeks Sets Leadership Team at Skydance TV

“It feels completely humbling,“ Abdy said of the recognition. “I am super proud to be a part of this organization and what it stands for and also be here to pass on whatever I can to the next generation. That is the most important thing to me.“

The honor was announced before her exit from Warner Bros., which took place as Paramount Skydance completed its $111 billion merger with Warner Bros. last month. During her tenure at the studio, Abdy oversaw a slate that included movies from female directors like Emerald Fennell, Maggie Gyllenhaal and Meyers; 2025 saw films directed by women drop to a seven-year low.

A subject that is being discussed with increasing alarm in industry circles, and was certainly a subject at Thursday night‘s WIF event, is the recent culling of top female executives during the ongoing layoffs and larger restructuring following the latest round of Hollywood mergers and acquisitions. In addition to Abdy, Cindy Holland exited her post as Paramount‘s streaming chief, while Bela Bajaria was ousted as Netflix’s chief content officer.

“Obviously, it is upsetting to see,“ Abdy offered of a raft of departures of female executives among Hollywood‘s top ranks. She went on to add: “But all of these women are incredible women and have incredible careers. These one moments don‘t define you. What defines you is the work you did and the work you left behind and the work you hope to do in the future. That‘s all we can keep doing, especially us executives, is try and support the next generation of storytellers and all of the artists.“

"It could have a strong impact not only on self-driving cars but also on drone positioning."

The launch of NASA's Artemis II mission in April 2026 caused significant disturbances in Earth's ionosphere that could have triggered temporary, localized errors in GPS positioning, a new study has found.

The study, by a team of researchers from National Cheng Kung University in Taiwan, analyzed data from high-precision networks of fixed, ground-based GPS receivers, used by U.S. scientific institutions to measure the minuscule motions of Earth's tectonic plates in the lead-up to earthquakes. By measuring how long it takes GPS signals to travel from space to ground stations, the researchers were able to reconstruct how the passage of the Artemis II mission's Space Launch System (SLS) rocket changed the concentrations of free electrons in the ionosphere — the electrically charged layer of Earth's atmosphere at altitudes above 30 miles (50 kilometers).

The measurements found that the ionospheric disturbances resulting from the sheer power of the Artemis II launch were more significant than any caused by other rocket launches to date and up to ten times more intense than those observed following the test launches of SpaceX's Starship, which is twice as powerful as the SLS based on liftoff thrust.

Artemis II saw humans return to the lunar space for the first time in more than fifty years, a mission that NASA hopes will pave the way for lunar landings and eventually the establishment of a sustained human presence on the moon.

During the mission's launch, ground-based GPS stations detected changes in the ionospheric electron density equivalent to positioning errors of several meters. Such inaccuracies could easily throw self-driving cars off track, potentially causing traffic collisions, according to Charles Lin, an earth science professor at National Cheng Kung University and one of the co-authors of the paper.

"A positioning error of a couple of meters is enough to cause an autonomous car to change lanes," Lin told Space.com. "It could have a strong impact not only on self-driving cars but also on drone positioning."

GPS receivers determine their position on Earth's surface at any single moment by measuring their distance to four different GPS satellites. When concentrations of free electrons in the upper atmosphere change — for example during a solar storm or after a rocket passage — the signal reaches Earth either faster or more slowly, resulting in inaccurate measurements.

Satellites of the U.S. GPS constellation and other Global Navigation Satellite Systems orbit Earth at an altitude of around 12,550 miles (20,200 kilometers), far above the upper edge of the ionosphere, meaning the positioning, navigation and timing signal these satellites transmit must pass through this volatile atmospheric layer to reach Earth.

Severe solar storms can disrupt GPS signals for days by dumping energy into the atmosphere in the form of charged particles from the sun. The impact of rocket launches, triggered by the supersonic flight of the rocket body through the high-altitude air, is much more short-lived. As the rocket soars up, it creates a shock wave, which virtually punches a hole into the ionosphere.

In the aftermath of the Artemis II launch, the researchers observed two such holes — one left behind by the 212-foot-long (65 meters) SSL core stage, and the other caused by two subsequent thruster burns of the rocket's upper stage. In both cases, these holes stretched across the American continent from East to West like giant 3,100-mile (5,000-kilometer) contrails.

Despite the enormous power of the SLS core stage, the disturbance caused by the second-stage burns directly inside the ionosphere was far more prominent.

Those two burns, at altitudes around 115 miles (185 kilometers), took place more than an hour after lift-off and allowed the Orion capsule to break free from Earth's gravity and head for the moon.

"Rocket launches from the ground to space produce that kind of effect, but we have never seen this kind of orbital maneuver in an interplanetary mission," said Lin. "In the future, as we are going to see many more missions going to the moon and to Mars, these space weather effects will become much more significant."

The study was published as a pre-print online in the journal Geophysical Research Letters.

#691. NASA discovers Jupiter’s invisible shield is more complex than Earth’s

NASA's Juno spacecraft has uncovered remarkable new details about how Jupiter withstands the constant stream of high-energy particles flowing from the Sun. The findings reveal that the solar system's largest planet relies on a much more complex system of plasma waves and shock regions than Earth does.

Led by scientists at the University of Iowa, the research provides the most detailed observations yet of Jupiter's bow shock, an invisible boundary where particles from the Sun encounter the planet's magnetic environment. The discovery reveals important differences in how Jupiter and Earth respond to these incoming particles.

Beyond Jupiter, the results could also help scientists understand some of the most powerful events in the universe, including the extreme shock waves associated with exploding stars.

How Jupiter Protects Itself From the Solar Wind

The Sun continuously releases a stream of electrically charged particles called the solar wind. These particles travel through space at tremendous speeds, often faster than the speed at which sound waves move through the surrounding plasma. When the solar wind approaches a planet with a magnetic field, it encounters a boundary known as the bow shock.

At Earth, this boundary plays an important protective role. It slows and heats the incoming particles, helping redirect much of the solar wind around the planet. Without this process, more harmful particles could reach Earth's atmosphere, potentially making conditions less favorable for life.

Jupiter also has a bow shock, but its enormous size, powerful magnetic field, and gaseous composition make it a particularly interesting place to study how these boundaries behave. Scientists have long wanted to understand whether Jupiter handles the solar wind differently from Earth and what those differences might reveal about other objects throughout the universe.

Scientists Discover a More Complex Defense System

Using measurements from Juno, researchers discovered that Jupiter relies on plasma waves with multiple frequencies to slow and heat incoming solar particles. These different frequencies, known as "harmonics," create a more elaborate wave pattern than the one typically observed at Earth.

The process can be compared to music. Just as several notes played together produce a richer sound than a single note, plasma waves containing multiple frequencies can interact with incoming particles in more complex ways. This allows Jupiter's bow shock to transfer energy to more particles, heating them and reducing their speed.

Earth's bow shock, by comparison, primarily uses plasma waves concentrated around a single frequency. That simpler arrangement is generally sufficient for the conditions encountered near our planet.

"Jupiter has found its own way to deal with the solar wind, through plasma waves that are stronger and exhibit richer harmonic structures," says Jayasri Joseph, a postdoctoral researcher in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at Iowa and the study's corresponding author. "That's important because if you have multiple frequencies, you can heat more particles in the solar wind and slow them down."

The researchers identified another striking difference in how the two planets interact with the solar wind.

Before incoming particles reach Jupiter's main bow shock, they can encounter smaller shock structures called shocklets. These additional regions help slow the solar wind before it arrives at the primary shock boundary.

Earth's bow shock, in contrast, generally serves as the main region where the incoming solar wind is slowed and redirected. Jupiter's additional shock structures reveal a more complicated process for managing the energy carried by solar particles.

"Earth does not need to take these extra steps to handle the solar wind because the impact isn't as powerful," says Bill Kurth, a research scientist in Iowa's Department of Physics and Astronomy and a coauthor of the study.

Kurth has participated in NASA's Juno mission since the spacecraft launched in 2011.

What Jupiter Can Teach Us About Exploding Stars

Although these observations focus on Jupiter, their significance could extend far beyond our solar system.

Shock waves occur throughout the universe, particularly in environments where enormous amounts of energy are released. Some of the most extreme examples are found in supernova remnants, the expanding clouds of material left behind when certain dying stars explode.

These cosmic shock waves are vastly more powerful than those encountered near Jupiter. However, the physical processes that control how energy moves through plasma share important similarities. By examining Jupiter's bow shock in unprecedented detail, scientists can investigate mechanisms that would be much harder to measure directly around distant stars.

"Because even more powerful shocks occur around astrophysical objects such as supernova remnants, Jupiter's bow shock offers a nearby natural laboratory for exploring and for understanding how nature converts enormous amounts of flow energy into heat and energetic particles," Joseph says.

Understanding these processes could improve scientific models of how shock waves transfer energy, heat particles, and shape environments across the universe.

NASA's Juno Makes Unprecedented Measurements

The breakthrough was made possible by observations Juno collected in December 2024. The NASA spacecraft has been orbiting Jupiter since July 2016, providing researchers with an extraordinary opportunity to investigate the giant planet and its surrounding environment.

A key part of the discovery came from the Juno Waves instrument, which was designed and built by physicists at the University of Iowa. The instrument measures electric and magnetic wave activity, allowing scientists to study the behavior of plasma around Jupiter.

Earlier spacecraft had detected the presence of bow shocks at outer planets, but they lacked the measurements needed to reveal the detailed structure of the plasma waves involved. Juno's observations have now provided a much clearer picture of how these waves behave at Jupiter.

The findings were published online on July 31 in Nature Communications in a study titled "Plasma wave observations from Juno spacecraft at the Jovian bow shock."

Additional contributors from the University of Iowa included Allison Jaynes, an associate professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy, along with Jeremy Faden and Chris Piker, who provide research support in the same department.

The international research team also included Lynn Wilson III of NASA Goddard Space Flight Center; John Connerney of NASA Goddard Space Flight Center and the Space Research Corporation; Frederic Allegrini of the Southwest Research Institute and the University of Texas-San Antonio; Rob Wilson of the University of Colorado-Boulder; Ali Sulaiman of the University of Minnesota; Scott Boltion and Robert Ebert of the Southwest Research Institute; and Barry Mauk of the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory.

Materials provided by University of Iowa. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

"It was like looking for a needle in a haystack."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have long suspected that Mars is geologically "dead," but new spacecraft observations suggest the Red Planet's volcanoes are merely sleeping.

That means that Olympus Mons, the extinct Martian volcano that at around 16 miles (26 kilometers) above the surrounding Martian plains is the largest mountain in the solar system, may in fact be a slumbering giant.

The observations were made with the European Space Agency (ESA) mission ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) as it studied volcanic fissures along the Alba Mons region of the Red Planet. Alba Mons is in the Tharsis region of Mars, the same area that is home to Olympus Mons. While the latter is the tallest volcano in the solar system, at 374 miles (600 km) across, about the size of Arizona, the Alba Mons region is the largest volcano when considering surface area.

TGO detected gas containing hydrogen chloride making its way to the surface of Mars through the Alba Mons fissures. The same gas is commonly found escaping from magmatic vents on Earth, with the compound coming from hot magma beneath the surface. Detecting it on Mars is a sign of dormant Martian volcanism.

Orbital imagery had previously shown some volcanoes appear to have been active within the last few million years, and seismometers have detected the rumbling of "marsquakes," both implying the Red Planet is volcanically active. However, eruptions and lava flows have been conspicuous by their absence.

"Our findings suggest that Mars has retained enough internal heat to support volcanic activity until recently, and possibly still does," team co-leader and scientist at the Space Research Centre of the Polish Academy of Sciences, Daniel Mège, said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. "The TGO was able to find the smoking gun. It was like looking for a needle in a haystack."

Mège and colleagues were first alerted to something strange happening on Mars when they noticed spikes of hydrogen chloride during Martian summer and on the northern hemisphere of the Red Planet. That is both a time and place at which hydrogen chloride shouldn't be detected.

The gas usually peaks in the northern hemisphere during winter on Mars, disappearing in the summer. This variation is connected to the water and dust cycle on Mars. An exception to the rule occurs over volcanic fissures on the flanks of the Alba Mons volcano, in early summer.

The TGO followed up on this by detecting fresh and narrow fissures, in some cases hundreds of feet long, in the Alba Mons region. A clear sign of volcanism.

"It's truly amazing that it spotted a handful of molecules from a perhaps intermittent source, whilst moving continuously along its orbit to monitor the whole Martian atmosphere," Mège said.

The team thinks that these gases have been rising from the interior of Mars during the Martian winter, becoming blocked by ice. When this ice sublimates, changes directly from solid to gas, during summer, the gas is released, prompting spikes in hydrogen chloride seen by the TGO.

"Looking at the spatial distribution of the seeping, it became instantly obvious to me that there was something volcanic behind it, but it had to be demonstrated," said Mège. "A huge part of the work consisted of examining all the possible chemical processes going on in the Martian atmosphere. "We needed to be rigorous, critical and creative to explain the presence of hydrogen chloride. The data were complex, but also excellent brain food."

Mège and colleagues theorize that the gas is connected to "volcanic plumbing" in the form of a dormant magma chamber under the surface of Mars.

Regions like this could become hotspots (pun not intended) in the search for life on Mars. That is because magmatic gases like hydrogen chloride would have been more abundant in the past, creating a thicker Martian atmosphere and warmer climate.

Not only would this have led to liquid water covering much of the Martian surface, but when lava bubbled through the Martian crust and met groundwater, warm habitable niches ideal for microbial life could have been forged.

"Looking for Martian life in the seeping fissures of the Alba Mons region would make a lot of sense. If hydrothermal systems are active, they could contain the ingredients and energy needed for microorganisms to develop, and shield microorganisms from the hostile and changing environment above the surface," Mège concluded.

The team's research was published in the journal Science Advances on Wednesday (Nov. 4).

#688. Can we regrow damaged seagrass meadows?

Seagrass protects coasts, shelters thousands of species and stores CO2. But some 30% of this valuable ecosystem has disappeared since the late 19th century. Can we bring it back?

Half a dozen divers are navigating the cold waters of the Baltic Sea off the coast of Dahme, a small beach town in northern Germany. Keeping the roots intact, conservationists carefully lift shoots from a donor meadow of seagrass and place them in a bag.

They only take a few shoots from each spot, which will be planted where the conservationists hope to regrow another meadow. They've already picked out a prime area for the young plants, which need sandy sediment, shelter from waves and currents and sufficient light and oxygen to thrive.

The scientists see the work as critical. Myriam Spicka, who heads the NGO Seagrass Conservation, says she has "seen the changes" in the more than 30 years she's been diving. And she is not the only one who has witnessed the destruction.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Scientists estimate that around 60% of the Baltic coast's seagrass meadows have disappeared.

"That's the bad news," said marine ecologist Thorsten Reusch from the GEOMAR Helmholtz Center for Ocean Research Kiel . "The good news is that the decline has stopped."

Underwater seagrass meadows feed and shelter fish, crabs, shellfish and many other species. They improve water quality and slow waves, helping protect shores from erosion. And they store carbon in the seabed about 30 to 50 times faster than forests.

Around 70 species of seagrass can be found along the coasts of more than 150 countries. Some grow just below the surface, others at depths of 60 meters or almost 200 feet.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Some countries have far more seagrass, particularly in the Indo-Pacific," said Reusch. "There, it can play a major role in their carbon balance."

But the value of seagrass goes beyond carbon storage. Its meadows in the Baltic are among the sea's most valuable habitats. They shelter wildlife, stabilize the seabed and act as natural filters by trapping particles and nutrients.

Planting individual seagrass shoots is painstaking work so people like Reinhard Helbig are trying to make it easier.

Through ZosteraTec, the start-up he co-founded, he helps restore marine habitats, including seagrass meadows damaged by offshore activity, such as wind farm construction. His work begins on the beach.

"Stormy weather helps us. Waves and currents wash seagrass out of the seabed. A day or two later, it washes up here, still fresh," he said.

The collected shoots are grown and multiplied in ZosteraTec's aquaculture. Several months later, the marine saplings are laid on a plant support. A specially developed machine binds the planted strands with biodegradable thread. The resulting lengths can be laid on the seabed with less diving work.

"We plant here on land to cut down on underwater work. That means fewer dives, and we can do the painstaking work on shore," Helbig said.

Researchers at the Geomar Helmholtz Center in Kiel are also testing new ways to restore seagrass across larger areas, including using seeds.

Marine ecologist Esther Thomsen reaches into an aquarium tank and pulls out a flowerpot containing seagrass.

"Ten percent of the plants in our meadows produce seeds. You can clearly see the seeds sitting inside the seed pod," she said.

"The big advantage of restoring meadows from seed is greater genetic diversity. And in the future, we should be able to sow seeds over much larger areas," explained Thomsen.

Reusch from Geomar said they currently "think the most promising way to grow meadows that can withstand climate change is to plant individual shoots as a foundation, then sow seeds between them to increase genetic diversity."

Whether a planting mission is successful is revealed months or even years later.

Thomsen and her colleagues are visiting the first seagrass meadow planted in Germany's Baltic waters in 2021. The divers count shoots, check how densely they grow and record how the meadow has developed.

They then compare it with the donor meadow that supplied the plants. Only that comparison reveals whether the new crop has merely survived or is beginning to function more like a natural one.

"We've just checked the seagrass meadow, and it's really dense. We counted lots of shoots per square," Thomsen said. "It's looking really good."

#687. Einstein's equations may explain the universe without dark energy

Mathematicians are raising a major challenge to one of modern cosmology's most widely accepted explanations: the idea that dark energy is driving the accelerating expansion of the universe.

A study published in Proceedings of the Royal Society A presents mathematical findings that researchers at the University of California, Davis, say reveal a fundamental instability in the standard model of the expanding universe. Their calculations suggest that cosmic acceleration could emerge naturally from Einstein's equations, potentially eliminating the need to invoke mysterious dark energy.

The work challenges the Lambda-cold dark matter model, the leading framework scientists use to describe the universe's evolution since the Big Bang. The researchers reached their conclusions by studying the Einstein-Euler equations, which combine Einstein's theory of general relativity with equations describing how fluids behave. Together, these mathematical tools help scientists investigate everything from galaxies and black holes to the expansion of the cosmos.

A Hidden Instability in Our Model of the Universe

To explain the problem, Blake Temple, the study's corresponding author and a distinguished professor emeritus of mathematics at UC Davis, offered a simple comparison: a pencil balanced vertically on its tip.

"All the forces are in balance when a pencil is standing on end, so it is a 'solution of the equations,'" he said. "But it's unstable. Any breath of air and it falls away."

According to Temple, the team's mathematical analysis shows that Friedmann spacetimes, which form the foundation of conventional models of cosmic expansion, are unstable at both small and large scales in the context of the Big Bang. He described the standard solution as exceptionally unstable.

"Unstable solutions in physics and science are considered not physical," Temple said. "You'll never observe them in nature."

This instability could have far-reaching consequences. If the universe naturally evolves away from the behavior predicted by these conventional models, its accelerating expansion might not require a separate form of energy to explain it. Instead, Temple argues, the answer could already be contained within Einstein's original theory of gravity.

"The instability of all Friedmann spacetimes to accelerated expansion suggests a simpler, more natural explanation for the acceleration of the universe than dark energy," he said.

Why Scientists Believe Dark Energy Is Expanding the Universe

For nearly three decades, dark energy has been the leading explanation for one of astronomy's most puzzling discoveries: the universe is not simply expanding, but its expansion is accelerating.

The concept has roots in Einstein's groundbreaking 1915 theory of general relativity, which describes gravity as the curvature of space and time. Einstein originally believed the universe was static, neither expanding nor contracting. To make his equations compatible with that assumption, he introduced a mathematical term that counteracted gravity, calling it the "cosmological constant."

That assumption changed after Edwin Hubble discovered evidence in 1929 that the universe was expanding. Einstein famously referred to his introduction of the cosmological constant as his "biggest blunder," since his original equations without the additional term could have predicted an expanding universe.

The cosmological constant returned to prominence in the 1990s, when astronomers discovered that cosmic expansion was speeding up. It became closely associated with dark energy, the name given to the unknown component thought to be responsible for this acceleration.

Today's standard cosmological framework builds on the Friedmann universe, a mathematical description in which space expands while matter remains evenly distributed across the cosmos at any given moment. This assumption of large-scale uniformity plays a central role in how scientists reconstruct the universe's history.

But Temple and his collaborators began questioning whether the underlying mathematics could remain stable, prompting them to investigate other possible explanations for the observed acceleration.

Could Einstein's Equations Explain Cosmic Acceleration?

The researchers initially considered whether a massive shockwave might help explain the universe's expansion and the unexpected acceleration associated with it.

"Our first idea was that maybe the universe was expanding because there was a shockwave, and the anomalous acceleration was the expanding wave behind that shockwave," Temple said. "Then we realized there's a family of self-similar solutions during the radiation epoch of the Big Bang, which might model that expanding wave."

In mathematics and physics, self-similar solutions describe patterns that retain their underlying structure when viewed at different scales. A familiar example is a fractal, in which similar shapes can appear at increasingly larger or smaller sizes.

The researchers identified a family of these solutions associated with the radiation-dominated period of the early universe, when radiation played a major role in determining how the cosmos evolved.

Building on their earlier work, they used a self-similar form of Einstein's equations to represent the standard cosmological model as a rest point, a mathematical state in which the system's defining variables remain unchanged. This approach allowed them to examine whether small departures from that state would disappear or grow over time.

Their analysis provided a mathematical framework for evaluating the stability of the standard model and, more broadly, Friedmann spacetimes during the matter-dominated era of the early universe, when matter became more influential than radiation.

A Mathematical Challenge to the Standard Big Bang Model

The results suggest that the conventional mathematical descriptions of the expanding universe are vulnerable to disturbances that grow rather than fade.

"We prove that, like Einstein's static model, the Friedmann spacetimes are all unstable to radial perturbation at large length scales," Temple said. "This appears to rule out the Lambda-cold dark matter model as a viable stable solution of the Einstein equations of general relativity, with or without dark energy."

Radial perturbations are disturbances that change with distance from a central point. In the researchers' mathematical framework, such changes can cause the behavior of an expanding universe to depart from the predictions of the standard Friedmann model.

"This means," he added, "that the Big Bang should generically look exactly like a Friedmann spacetime near the center of symmetry, but generically one should observe accelerations away from Friedmann far from the center."

In other words, the universe could behave much like the standard model predicts near a central region while exhibiting different expansion behavior farther away.

The researchers argue that this instability may offer a natural route to accelerated cosmic expansion without adding a cosmological constant or invoking dark energy. Their calculations indicate that the acceleration can emerge directly from the Einstein-Euler equations themselves.

The findings represent a theoretical challenge to standard cosmology rather than observational proof that dark energy is unnecessary. Establishing whether this alternative can describe the actual universe would require determining how well its predictions match astronomical observations.

Does the Universe Have a Special Location?

Beyond the dark energy question, the study also raises a more fundamental issue involving the Copernican principle.

Named after astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus, who helped overturn the belief that Earth sits at the center of the solar system, the principle holds that our location in the universe is not fundamentally special or privileged.

This assumption has become an important part of modern cosmology, supporting the view that the universe looks broadly similar when observed from different locations on sufficiently large scales.

The researchers' alternative mathematical framework introduces a center of spherical symmetry, raising questions about where an observer would need to be located for the model to agree with observations.

Temple argues that the Copernican principle must be applied consistently when evaluating competing explanations of the universe.

"Both the Lambda-cold dark matter model and a spherically symmetric spacetime produce a special place where we must lie for the model to be physically plausible," Temple said. "If this principle rules out one, it has to rule out the other."

The work opens another avenue for investigating why the universe's expansion is accelerating. Although dark energy remains a central component of the prevailing cosmological model, the researchers contend that the mathematics of general relativity may offer a different explanation for the same phenomenon.

If further theoretical and observational work supports their interpretation, it could lead to a significant reassessment of how scientists understand cosmic expansion and the mathematical foundations of the Big Bang.

The research received funding from the United Kingdom's Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council and the American Institute of Mathematics SQuaREs Program.

Swift had a pretty good 22-year run, but NASA wanted the scope to keep going even longer.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Swift space telescope has reached the end of its long and winding road.

Swift fell uncontrolled to Earth today (Nov. 4), 22 years after it launched but just three months after a private spacecraft was supposed to boost it to a higher, life-extending orbit.

The 3,200-pound (1,450 kilograms) observatory reentered Earth's atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST (1239 GMT) today over northern Sumatra, according to satellite tracker Jonathan McDowell, who cited U.S. Space Force data. The fall likely didn't make much of an impact; NASA officials predicted beforehand that most of the minibus-sized Swift would burn up as it fell, and they put the odds of any of the surviving pieces hurting anyone on Earth at just 1 in 2,100.

Several videos circulating on social media appear to show the spacecraft's fiery reentry, though it has yet to be independently verified.

Likely reentry of @NASA's #Swift observatory over Sumatra & Malaysia at 12:39 UTC today.November 4, 2026

Likely reentry of @NASA's #Swift observatory over Sumatra & Malaysia at 12:39 UTC today.November 4, 2026

Swift — officially known as the Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer — launched to Earth orbit in November 2004 on a two-year mission to study gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), the most powerful explosions in the universe. "Swift" was not an acronym but rather referred to the spacecraft's observational agility.

"Swift needed to detect and locate gamma-ray bursts, communicate their position to other observatories, and then swing its telescopes around to image the burst locations before their afterglows faded out," S. Bradley Cenko, Swift's principal investigator (PI) at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, said in an Oct. 23 statement. "This typically took Swift about a minute to do."

Swift didn't just observe GRBs. It also studied a variety of other cosmic bodies and phenomena, from faraway supernova explosions and feeding black holes to asteroids and comets in our own solar system.

And it kept doing this long after its warranty expired — for about 20 years after, in fact. The space telescope didn't conduct its final science observation until this past Oct. 20. (Swift underwent a name change during this stretch: In 2018, it was rechristened the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory after its first PI, who died the previous year.)

"Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long," Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of NASA's Astrophysics Division, said in the same Oct. 23 statement.

"In that time, Swift played a major role in advancing our understanding of the changing universe and was part of a revolution in astrophysics that showed how critical rapid-response observations are to the entire community," he added.

Swift was incredibly productive, observing more than 2,000 GRBs and 1,400 supernovas over the course of its long scientific life. But it could have gathered even more data, had a dramatic rescue mission worked out.

In September 2025, NASA awarded the Arizona company Katalyst Space a $30 million contract to design, launch and operate a robotic spacecraft that would meet up with Swift and boost it to a higher orbit, thus extending its operational life.

Swift was falling back to Earth: It had no onboard thrusters to counteract the effect of atmospheric drag, which had been pulling the observatory down ever since it launched. The process was accelerating as Swift got lower, so Katalyst had to work fast. And the company did: It launched its refrigerator-sized, three-armed LINK servicing spacecraft on July 3, targeting an August capture of Swift.

That didn't happen, however. LINK suffered problems with its propulsion system and orientation-maintaining reaction wheels, which nixed the planned meetup. Still, it was a worthwhile effort, according to NASA.

"From the beginning, this was a high-risk, high-reward mission," Domagal-Goldman said in a statement on Sept. 25, the day that LINK itself crashed back to Earth.

"And while we'll be sad to see Swift's mission come to a close, we knew this boost effort would be worthwhile either way — advancing U.S. spacecraft servicing technology, challenging us to meet unprecedented mission timelines, and testing how we operate satellites to extend their time in low Earth orbit," he added.

Swift's crash today wasn't exactly unusual, by the way. At least three large objects — dead satellites or spent rocket bodies — fall back to Earth every day on average, a 2025 report found. And that number is bound to rise in the coming years, as humanity builds out more and more megaconstellations in Earth orbit.

Editor's note: This article was updated on Nov. 5 at 4:45 a.m. EST (0944 GMT) to include social media videos that may show the spacecraft's fiery demise.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

#685. Foot Fetish Encounter Leaves a Body in the Freezer in Singapore Dark Comedy Taiwan Creative Content Fest Project ‘Build to Order’

A young Singaporean couple who sell pictures of the wife’s feet online end up with a corpse in their freezer in “Build to Order,” the debut feature from director Huang Junxiang, which is at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei this week.

Singaporean couple Penny and Allan both work in real estate. They wed young so they could get a public housing flat, but property prices that keep climbing still leave them strapped. To bring in extra money, they put photos of Penny’s feet up for sale online. Then a rich client with a foot fetish offers them a staggering amount for the chance to suck her toes face to face, and they say yes. Related Stories Neon Partners With 'NAZA' Filmmakers, Guardian and MK2 to Bring Prize-Winning Doc to Wider Audiences Japan IP Market to Return to Cannes in 2027 as Tokyo Partnership Continues

The meeting goes badly wrong. The man suffers an allergic reaction, Allan’s amateur attempt at first aid fails and the client dies. In a panic, the couple stash him in their freezer. Months on, his widow, who has no idea what happened, taps them to list her luxury mansion – drawing the pair ever deeper into greed and guilt as they scramble to save themselves.

“When I was looking to buy my first home in Singapore, every property agent I met warned me that making the wrong decision would cost me financially in the long haul,” Huang says. “They said that I can’t make an emotional decision, I needed to make a logical one. In an expensive society like Singapore, I feel that many decisions are made rationally, at the cost of our identities and our relationships.”

The film is now in post-production, and Huang says finishing it has his full attention.

“I hope our audiences will be entertained by this dark comedy with genre moments and think a little more about the choices they make and the lives they want to lead,” he says.

Producer Macarius Chia says the film deals with a subject that resonates around the world – housing prices and what it costs to get by. “We were also entertained by the humorous script which takes the story in a few surprising directions, without losing sight of the character’s journey.”

Executive producer Lim Teck says he believes in Huang’s vision and that the film could become a breakout hit out of Singapore, “where housing and climbing the social ladder are always such hot topics.” Lim adds that the film is reasonably budgeted and has commercial potential.

In Taipei, the team wants to raise gap financing to finish post, along with partners for audio post and color grading. Chia says they also hope to find “a like-minded international sales agent who believes in the project as the story is accessible.”

For Lim, TCCF is a chance to introduce the project to friends across Asia’s film industry. “We believe our film has a chance to travel and do well in various Asian markets,” he says.

The Taiwan Creative Content Fest, organized by the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA), runs Nov. 6–9 at the Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center.

#684. Gen Z protests in Germany: Is France-style violence looming?

Young people in Germany are preparing to protest over education and climate change. Politicians fear violence like in France, but an expert sees differences.

As politicians in Germany look ahead to the coming weekend, many fear that cities across the country could witness the kind of violent unrest that recently shook France. An initiative known as "Gen Z regelt" ("Gen Z sorts it") has launched a social media campaign calling for demonstrations in 23 cities nationwide.

"Gen Z" broadly refers to the generation born between 1995 and 2010. Many feel that their parents' generation has done too little to combat climate change and has allowed the gap between rich and poor to widen ever further. At the same time, they are concerned about their educational prospects and future opportunities.

In France, what began as largely peaceful protests recently spiraled into serious unrest. Cars were set alight in several towns, while in Limoges the town hall was torched. In Lille, Lyon, and Toulouse and elsewhere, police deployed tear gas, leading to numerous arrests.

Many politicians, particularly within Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), are warning of similar scenes this coming weekend.

Alexander Throm, the CDU parliamentary group's domestic spokesperson, told the daily Handelsblatt newspaper: "Scenes like those in France must be prevented at all costs."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Throm's view, far-left groups and criminals from immigrant communities could "hijack" the demonstrations. "An ominous alliance is emerging, particularly in Berlin," he warned.

Marc Henrichmann, also of the CDU, chair of the Bundestag's parliamentary oversight panel for the intelligence services, also expressed concern: "The far-left extremist scene is internationally connected and coordinated." He said that violent far-left activists now even cross national borders to engage in looting and acts of violence elsewhere.

But Sebastian Koos, sociologist at the University of Konstanz whose research focuses on youth and protest movements, told DW that he does not expect Germany to experience unrest on a scale comparable to that seen in France, even though events in the neighboring country helped spark the protests now being planned across Germany.

Koos sees key differences between young people in the two countries. "Unlike in France, these protests are not driven by the same level of anger," he said. "They have been planned, officially registered and carefully organized. The website, in particular, places strong emphasis on peaceful protest and repeatedly stresses a non-violent approach."

At the same time, the sociologist does not rule out the possibility that extremist groups could exploit the authorized demonstrations to stir up unrest: "It is certainly very important for the police and public authorities to be well prepared."

Quentin Gärtner, 19, studies biotechnology in Heidelberg and served until November of last year as secretary-general of the Federal Student Conference, which represents around 7.5 million school students in Germany.

"What unites us is that we have run out of patience with the education system. Many young people are deeply frustrated," he told DW. "The performance of German school students continues to decline, teaching positions are constantly being cut, and in many cases school buildings have seen little or no meaningful investment for years."

For Gärtner, the discontent reflects a broader problem with parliamentary democracy in Germany and many other Western countries.

"Politicians want to win elections. They focus on the groups that matter most to them electorally rather than on the future and the long-term sustainability of their policies," he said.

"And in our aging societies, older people and the baby boomer generation are the groups that carry the most political weight."

Opposition parties in Germany have also voiced understanding for the concerns of younger people. Speaking to Germany's public broadcaster ZDF, Green Party co-leader Felix Banaszak said: "The intergenerational contract is no longer working. Older generations have driven the climate into a dead end."

He argued that the social welfare system was also reaching its limits and that rents had become unaffordable. According to Banaszak, the only thing the state seems to offer young people are the letters sent to 18-year-olds asking them to consider joining the military. Germany is currently desperate to expand the Bundeswehr and is considering reintroducing national service.

By Tuesday, around 134,000 people had registered on the "Gen Z regelt" website to take part in the protests planned for the coming Saturday. With several days still to go before the demonstrations, that number could rise further.

#683. Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging

Sugar substitutes are often promoted as a healthier way to enjoy sweet foods and drinks without consuming as much sugar. However, new research suggests that some of these widely used sweeteners may have an unexpected downside for long-term brain health.

A study published in Neurology, the medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology, found that people who consumed the most low- and no-calorie sweeteners experienced significantly faster declines in memory and thinking skills than those who consumed the least. The association was particularly pronounced among people with diabetes.

Researchers examined seven sweeteners commonly used in foods and beverages: aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, xylitol, sorbitol and tagatose. These ingredients frequently appear in ultra-processed products, including diet sodas, flavored waters, energy drinks, yogurt and low-calorie desserts. Some are also sold separately for sweetening foods and beverages.

"Low- and no-calorie sweeteners are often seen as a healthy alternative to sugar; however, our findings suggest certain sweeteners may have negative effects on brain health over time," said study author Claudia Kimie Suemoto, MD, PhD, of the University of São Paulo in Brazil.

Importantly, the findings show an association rather than a proven cause-and-effect relationship. Researchers cannot conclude from this study that consuming these sweeteners directly damages the brain or causes memory loss.

Study Tracks Nearly 13,000 Adults for Eight Years

To investigate whether sugar substitutes might be connected to cognitive health, researchers analyzed data from 12,772 adults across Brazil. Participants were 52 years old on average when the study began and were followed for approximately eight years.

At the beginning of the study, participants completed detailed dietary questionnaires describing the foods and drinks they had consumed during the previous year. Researchers used these responses to estimate each person's daily intake of the seven sweeteners.

Participants were then separated into three groups according to how much of the sweeteners they consumed. Those in the lowest consumption group averaged 20 milligrams per day (mg/day), while those in the highest group averaged 191 mg/day. For comparison, 191 milligrams of aspartame is roughly the amount found in one can of diet soda.

Of the seven sweeteners examined, sorbitol had the highest average intake, at 64 mg/day. Sorbitol belongs to a category of sweeteners called sugar alcohols, which provide sweetness and are commonly used as sugar substitutes.

Throughout the study, participants completed cognitive assessments at three points: the beginning, middle, and end. These tests measured several abilities essential for everyday mental functioning, including memory, language, and the speed at which the brain processes information.

Researchers evaluated verbal fluency, or the ability to quickly retrieve and produce words, along with working memory, which allows people to temporarily hold and use information. They also tested word recall and processing speed to determine how these abilities changed over time.

High Sweetener Consumption Linked to 62% Faster Cognitive Decline

The results revealed a striking difference between people who consumed the most sweeteners and those who consumed the least.

After accounting for factors that could influence cognitive health, including age, sex, high blood pressure, and cardiovascular disease, researchers found that participants in the highest consumption group experienced a 62% faster decline in overall thinking and memory abilities compared with those in the lowest group.

That difference was equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of cognitive aging over the study period.

Even moderate consumption was associated with measurable differences. Participants in the middle group experienced a 35% faster decline than those consuming the least, equivalent to roughly 1.3 additional years of cognitive aging.

These estimates describe changes in cognitive test performance rather than a direct measurement of biological brain aging. They also do not mean that everyone who consumes artificial sweeteners will experience memory problems.

Stronger Links Found in Adults Under 60 and People With Diabetes

When researchers examined different age groups, they discovered that the association was not consistent across all participants.

Among adults younger than 60, higher sweetener consumption was linked to faster declines in verbal fluency and overall cognitive performance. However, researchers did not find a similar association among participants older than 60.

The relationship was also stronger in people with diabetes than in those without the condition. This finding is especially relevant because people with diabetes frequently turn to sugar substitutes to help manage their sugar intake.

Examining the sweeteners individually revealed another important distinction. Six of the seven substances were associated with faster declines in overall cognitive performance, particularly memory.

Those six were aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, sorbitol and xylitol.

Tagatose was the exception. Researchers found no association between its consumption and cognitive decline in this study. However, that finding does not establish that tagatose protects the brain or is necessarily safer than other sweeteners.

Should People Rethink Artificial Sweeteners?

The findings raise important questions about whether replacing sugar with low-calorie alternatives always delivers the health benefits consumers expect, particularly when it comes to the brain.

"While we found links to cognitive decline for middle-aged people both with and without diabetes, people with diabetes are more likely to use artificial sweeteners as sugar substitutes," Suemoto said. "More research is needed to confirm our findings and to investigate if other refined sugar alternatives, such as applesauce, honey, maple syrup or coconut sugar, may be effective alternatives."

Researchers also acknowledged several limitations. The analysis did not cover every artificial sweetener available on the market, so the findings cannot necessarily be applied to all sugar substitutes.

In addition, dietary information came from participants' own recollections of what they had eaten and drunk. Because people may forget foods, underestimate portions, or inaccurately report their habits, these estimates may not perfectly reflect actual sweetener consumption.

The observational design also means that other factors could help explain the relationship between sweetener intake and cognitive decline, despite researchers' efforts to account for several important health differences.

Further studies will be needed to determine whether the sweeteners themselves contribute to changes in brain function, why certain groups appear more strongly affected, and whether different sugar alternatives produce different long-term outcomes.

The research was supported by the Brazilian Ministry of Health, the Ministry of Science, Technology, and Innovation, and the National Council for Scientific and Technological Development.

Materials provided by American Academy of Neurology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

How "Forrest Gump", pizza, and a massive supporting cast of furballs came together to make one of "Star Trek"'s finest hours.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When "Star Trek" celebrated its 60th anniversary in September, it was a strangely muted affair. Sure, there were fan events, screenings, and even an attempt at a world record for the biggest simultaneous Vulcan salute in history, but the lack of a "Doctor Who"-style birthday episode felt like a glaring omission. It was like everyone had shown up for the party, but the organizers had forgotten to book the headline entertainment.

Luckily, there were rather more fireworks for the show's 30th birthday, when both "Voyager" and "Deep Space Nine" marked the occasion in style. "Voyager" episode "Flashback" took Tuvok (Tim Russ) back to his days on the USS Excelsior bridge alongside Original Series vets Hikaru Sulu (George Takei) and Janice Rand (Grace Lee Whitney).

But it was "DS9"'s "Trials and Tribble-ations" that turned out to be the more memorable voyage to "Trek" past, as Captain Benjamin Sisko (Avery Brooks) — with the help of some then-state-of-the-art digital trickery — came face-to-face with a young Captain James T. Kirk (William Shatner).

While "Flashback" aired within days of "Trek"'s September 8 birthday, fans had to wait a little longer for "DS9"'s contribution to the celebrations. Showrunner Ira Steven Behr was keen to avoid disrupting the space station-set drama's story arc for a comedic diversion, meaning that "Trials and Tribble-ations" didn't debut until November 4, 1996.

In the wake of "Flashback" — not to mention Spock and Scotty's comebacks in "The Next Generation" stories "Unification" and "Relics" — the "DS9" writers' room had already decided they needed to take a very different approach.

Early on, "Battlestar Galactica" creator Ronald D. Moore pitched a follow-up to Original Series episode "A Piece of the Action" (aka the one where the residents of Iotia brought 1920s gangsters to life). In an extremely meta concept that predated "Galaxy Quest" by three years, the story would have taken the Enterprise crew to a planet of Kirk and Spock impersonators.

"For the thirtieth anniversary, you go back, and you're basically going back to the planet of 'Star Trek' fans," Moore recalled in "The Fifty-Year Mission" by Mark A. Altman and Edward Gross. "They have conventions; they know all the adventures. It's a phenomenon, and you could comment on 'Star Trek' as a whole. I thought it would be interesting. But [fellow writer] René Echevarria thought it was a dangerous show to do, that we would be talking down to the fans on some level, and perhaps it wasn't the best way to go."

Instead, Echevarria suggested telling a story in the vein of Woody Allen's "Zelig" or "Forrest Gump" (then a zeitgeisty, multi-Oscar-winning box-office smash) and integrating the "Deep Space Nine" crew with the events of an Original Series episode.

"I thought, 'What bigger treat could there be than to go back into the past and board the original Enterprise and have a mission there?'" Echevarria said in a 1996 making-of documentary. "And Ron immediately said, 'It's gotta be "The Trouble with Tribbles!"'"

"The Trouble with Tribbles", a 1967 episode from "Star Trek"'s second season, is one of the most famous in the franchise's history. As well as featuring some minor scuffles with Klingons, it sees the Enterprise and Deep Space Station K-7 infested with the eponymous tribbles — cute, cuddly furballs of calm that reproduce at a dangerously exponential rate.

In "Trials and Tribble-ations", a timey-wimey incident involving the Bajoran Orb of Time transports the USS Defiant (one of the best "Star Trek" spaceships) back to the era of Kirk and Spock's famous five-year mission.

As Sisko recounts the adventure to a pair of agents from Starfleet's Department of Temporal Investigations (named Dulmur and Lucsly in homage to "The X-Files"), we learn how he, Dax (Terry Farrell), O'Brien (Colm Meaney), and Bashir (Alexander Siddig) spent a day playing Original Series cosplay on Kirk's Enterprise. It's "Star Trek"'s answer to "Back to the Future: Part II", as the crew interacts with established events while taking pains not to mess with history.

Although most of the guest stars from "The Trouble with Tribbles" had passed away over the intervening decades, one actor who'd played a pivotal role was still around. By the time he turned up in "Star Trek", 20-something stand-up comedian Charlie Brill had already brushed shoulders with pop-culture legend, having shared the bill with the Beatles when they made their famous appearance on "The Ed Sullivan Show" in February 1964.

Three years later he'd swapped Lennon and McCartney for Kirk and Spock, playing a Klingon spy masquerading as human Arne Darvin, whose cover is ultimately blown by the famously Klingon-phobic tribbles. In the newer episode, the older Darvin travels back in time to assassinate Kirk, plotting his revenge with a bomb implanted in an unfortunate tribble. Thwarting the evil scheme — and preserving the timeline — forms the basis of Sisko's mission.

Brill's return was seemingly written in the stars. When planning the episode, Behr and the other writers met for lunch at Mulberry Street Pizza in Beverly Hills and noted that the actor was alive and still working in the business. Then, just as they were talking about him, they happened to spot Brill across the very same restaurant.

"What were the chances that we would be talking about this old TV episode from 30 years ago, and the guy who we were talking about to bring back on the show would be standing there ordering a slice of pizza?" Behr recalled at the Trek Talks telethon (via TrekMovie).

But however strong its story, "Trials and Tribble-ations" was always going to live and die by its recreation of ' 60s-era "Trek". The production team subsequently pulled out all the stops, with Behr suggesting at the time that it may have been the most expensive hour of TV ever made.

The actors were kitted out in era-appropriate primary-colored outfits and given '60s hairdos. The make-up team also recreated the appearance of the Original Series' Klingons, whose very different look — "We do not discuss it with outsiders," says Worf — would later be explained away in a "Star Trek: Enterprise" two-parter.

The late Walter Koenig (who'd featured as Chekov in "The Trouble with Tribbles") showed the younger officers how to flip open a communicator, and the stunt team choreographed fights to look like the cheesy, Western-inspired brawls of a bygone era.

Behind the scenes, production designer Michael Okuda and his team used a mixture of original plans and scans of the episodes to painstakingly recreate the sets, while the visual effects team constructed an exact half-scale replica of the original 11-foot Enterprise shooting model housed in the Smithsonian.

The biggest magic trick, however, was dependent on CG technology — then very much in its infancy — making everyone believe that Sisko and co were walking the same corridors as Kirk. VFX supervisor Gary Hutzel had provided proof-of-concept early in the process:

"He showed us a clip from the old show," said Behr. "We looked at it and said, 'Okay, that looks good, but what does that have to do with us?' And he said, 'Well, you see that guy coming in through the door? That's not from the 1967 episode. That's one of our people!'"

Shooting in front of blue- and green-screens, the actors' performances were meticulously matched to the Original Series episode. Early on, Moore had identified two sequences from "The Trouble with Tribbles" that would be perfect for selling the concept: Kirk dressing down a line-up of officers after a bar room brawl and Tribbles raining down on Kirk from a storage container.

O'Brien and Bashir were digitally pasted over the original actors in the former, while the latter was explained away by Sisko and Dax's madcap dash to find the elusive explosive tribble. In most other shots, the DS9ers became background observers in existing scenes.

But there were still debates to be had over whether the two captains should meet. "It led to one of the most vociferous arguments we've had," said Behr, a passionate advocate for the "yes" camp. "We were so deadlocked, and there was so much emotion in the air, we actually turned to the writer intern and said, ‘What do you think?’ End of stalemate. Of course, being an intern and being a smart guy, he sided with his executive producer. And life went on." (The scene in which Sisko hands Kirk a duty roster for approval was actually lifted from another Original Series episode, "Mirror, Mirror", with Brooks replacing Barbara Luna (Lt. Marlena Moreau) on the bridge.)

It was all worth the effort. "Trials and Tribble-ations" was the most-watched episode of "DS9"'s fifth season, bagged nominations for three Emmys and a Hugo, and is now widely regarded as one of the best "Trek" episodes of all time.

David Gerrold, who wrote "The Trouble with Tribbles" and appeared as an extra in "Trials and Tribble-ations", described it as "possibly the best episode of 'Star Trek' after the Original Series," and various members of the writers' room have described it as a highlight of their time on the final frontier.

"From the writers to the director to the lighting, costumes, the set, sound effects, visual effects — everybody really put in so much time on that episode to really recreate the original Enterprise in any way they possibly could," said Moore. "Everybody was staring at film clips, doing research into [prop/costume] materials. It was a mania, and everybody just threw themselves into it. They wanted to make it great. And it shows."

'The Trouble with Tribbles' and 'Trials and Tribble-ations' are available to stream on Paramount+ in both the US and UK.

#681. Salon.com Shuts Down Cultural and Political Site After 31 Years

Salon.com, the website that became popular in the early days of the internet offering cultural commentary, progressive political analysis, lifestyle content and more, is shutting down, the company announced Thursday.

“When Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing,” the editorial team wrote in a statement. Related Stories Letterboxd in Negotiations to Be Acquired by New York Times Company Cate Blanchett-Backed Group and Collection of Hollywood Stars File Brief in New York Times-OpenAI Lawsuit: Hollywood Has ‘Proven Infrastructure’ to License Content

The San Francisco-based site was known for launching numerous writers’ careers and was a daily stop for many readers in the days before social media. Among the film critics that wrote for Salon were Stephanie Zacharek, Andrew O’Hehir and Charles Taylor. The site’s television writers and critics included Heather Havrilesky, Hanh Nguyen, Maureen Ryan and Melanie McFarland.

Salon joins later-arriving sites such as Buzzfeed and Gawker that found it difficult to monetize cultural and topical reporting for a general audience and eventually shut down.

“The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years,” the editors continued in their statement. “After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.

“Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.

“Thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege,” the statement concluded.
